title: Accurate divine science useful and laudable though not required for salvation
source_text: XXVIII. Denique etsi doceant ad salutem sufficere, si quis implicite credat pleraque fidei dogmata, neque putent ad salutem necessario requiri primorum etiam & praecipuorum articulorum fidei accuratam & distinctam notitiam, sed rudem tantum & confusam, nihilominus non negant utilem & laudabilem esse scientiam rerum divinarum, quippe quae amorem Dei magis ac magis accendit: & sicut laude digni sunt qui discendo proficiunt, ita merito reprehendi, qui semper discunt, & ad scientiam veritatis nunquam perveniunt.
pass_a_gloss: Finally, although they teach that it suffices for salvation if someone believes most dogmas of faith only implicitly, and do not think an accurate and distinct notitia even of the first and principal articles is necessarily required for salvation, but only a rude and confused one, nevertheless they do not deny that knowledge of divine things is useful and laudable, since it kindles the love of God more and more; and just as those who advance by learning are worthy of praise, so those who are always learning and never arrive at the knowledge of the truth deserve to be blamed.
pass_b_english: Even while holding that implicit faith in most dogmas, and only rude confused notitia of the principal articles, can suffice for salvation, Rome does not deny the usefulness of deeper divine science.
Such science kindles love of God; learners who advance deserve praise, while perpetual learners who never reach truth deserve blame.
